description: LZ77 back-references create data dependencies where output bytes depend on previously decompressed bytes. After parallel Huffman decoding resolves all literal/length/distance triples, a second pass must resolve these chains. Wavefront parallelism processes independent chains simultaneously: references pointing to already-resolved regions can execute immediately, creating a wavefront that propagates through the dependency graph.
mathematical_formalization: Model LZ77 output as a DAG G=(V,E) where V = {output positions} and (u,v) in E iff position v back-references position u. The wavefront at step t is W_t = {v : all predecessors of v in union_{i<t} W_i}. W_0 = {literals}. Decompression depth = longest path in G. For typical data, depth is O(log n) due to short reference chains. Sitaridi's MRR: iterate resolution rounds, each round resolving one level of indirection. Work O(n * d) where d = max chain depth.
analogical_connections: Like topological sort execution: process nodes whose dependencies are satisfied
Analogous to relaxation methods in numerical PDE solvers: wavefront sweeps resolve local dependencies iteratively
Similar to instruction scheduling in out-of-order processors: execute instructions whose operands are ready
implementation_hypothesis: After Huffman decode pass produces array of (literal | ref(len, dist)) entries, build a dependency bitvector: bit i is set if position i is a literal or its reference target is already resolved. Process all set positions in parallel using SIMD scatter/gather. Mark newly resolved positions. Iterate until all resolved. For most data, 3-5 rounds suffice. Use Sitaridi's MRR algorithm adapted for CPU SIMD.
experiment_seed: Profile LZ77 reference chain depth across Silesia corpus. Implement multi-round resolution on AVX-512 with 64-byte scatter/gather. Measure: (1) rounds needed to full resolution, (2) throughput vs. sequential memcpy-based decode, (3) impact of compression level (higher level = deeper chains). Compare to Sitaridi's GPU results scaled to CPU.
